title: Frozen Four: Denver stuns Michigan with an instant-classic, double-overtime victory
author: Scott Wheeler
content:
LAS VEGAS — This was a hellacious heavyweight matchup that lived up to the hype.

An instant classic.

Can they play again tomorrow?

The University of Denver (10) and the University of Michigan (nine) are the college hockey programs with the most national titles, and each team played a game worthy of reaching Saturday’s final. This one was fast, physical and had many highlight-reel saves. Several players were oh-so-close to being the hero. Just ask the Pioneers’ Rieger Lorenz, a Minnesota Wild prospect, who hit the crossbar on a redirection with eight minutes left in the first overtime.

In the end, it was captain Kent Anderson who finished a slick feed from Kristian Epperson with 7:25 left in double overtime to lift the Pioneers to a 4-3 victory over Michigan at T-Mobile Arena. Denver, playing for its third national title in five years, will face Wisconsin, 2-1 winner over North Dakota, in Saturday’s final.

“I don’t score many goals, so this is ranking up top so far,” Anderson said. “It means everything to play in this national championship game.”

All the Pioneers do is win. And this time, they had freshman goalie Johnny Hicks largely to thank. Hicks racked up 49 saves in a herculean performance and is 15-0-1 since taking over as the starter at midseason. The Wolverines, in their fifth Frozen Four since 2011, lost in the semifinals for the fifth straight time. They were hoping for their first title since 1998, but that drought will have to linger at least another year.

“We outshot them 43-16 in the last four periods. I thought we were outstanding, and we fought the whole time,” Michigan coach Brandon Naurato said. “In hockey and in life, sometimes you do it the right way, and you just don’t get the bounces. It’s a lot of pain right now, but I couldn’t be more proud. It didn’t feel like this in some of the past losses. I felt like we deserved it.”

It looked like the Wolverines were going to pull this one in regulation after Jayden Perron scored a power-play goal from the top of the left circle with nine minutes left. But the Pioneers battled back, with freshman Clarke Caswell tipping in a pass with just under three minutes left to force overtime.

The Pioneers took a 1-0 lead midway through the first period on a goal by Kyle Chyzowski. But Michigan bounced back with two goals in 59 seconds, with the second coming from coveted NHL prospect T.J. Hughes. Cale Ashcroft tied it back up for Denver just under three minutes into the second, and it was pretty evenly played from there on.

The two freshman goalies were terrific, with Hicks recovering from a scary collision with Malcom Spence early in the third. Hicks went down on the ice for a few minutes before staying in the game. He could have been the Game’s No. 1, No. 2 and No. 3 star. Michigan’s Jack Ivankovic was also very good in trying to mimic idol Marty Turco.

The third period was more back and forth, with Denver having a couple of power plays before Michigan converted. Denver was 0-for-5 on the power play, which could have been a key factor in this game. Michigan was 1-for-2.

Denver, which won titles in 2022 and 2024, was in its third Frozen Four in four years.

Going up against Michigan’s star goalie Ivankovic, who was drafted by Nashville in the second round in 2025, Denver’s Hicks left an impression Thursday.

Hicks took over as the Pioneers’ starter in January when Quentin Miller went out with an injury. All he did was go 14-0-1 to backstop Denver to the Frozen Four. On Thursday night, Hicks was dialed in. He moves like a jitterbug in the crease, anticipates passes well and reacts quickly when the puck takes unexpected bounces, and Michigan created plenty of those.

“Obviously, he was our best player tonight,” Denver coach David Carle said. “Very unfazed by the moment. Made a lot of great saves.”

Hicks was bowled over by Spence early in the third period, was very slow to get up but stayed in the game and held the Pioneers in the game despite Michigan’s taking over in terms of possession, shots and chances. He made an incredible save on a rebound in front of the net in overtime, popping back to his skates and exploding across the net for a pad stop on a shot from point-blank range.

If he were a few inches taller, Hicks would be on the NHL’s radar. If he keeps playing as he did down the stretch and Thursday, perhaps he should be anyway. — Jesse Granger

The Perron who zipped around making skill plays all over the ice for Michigan on Thursday night looks nothing like the one who played for North Dakota the two seasons prior and a lot more like the one Steel staff and USHL players used to tell me was one of the smartest, most skilled players they’d worked with or played against.

This was a make-or-break season for the gifted Carolina Hurricanes third-round pick, and the transfer to Michigan for his junior year felt like a chance for him to rewrite his story. He was the most noticeable player on the puck for either team Thursday, well before he scored to give Michigan a 3-2 lead. He was on his toes. He was catching defensemen with his speed and crossovers off the rush. He was making guys miss on cuts laterally. He looked like he was processing spacing and timing faster than everyone else. He was taking every puck to inside ice or the net (a far cry from his perimeter play at North Dakota). And his creativity and cleverness flashed on some really slick, eyes-in-the-back-of-his-head sequences.

“He’s a student of the game, he’s a hockey nerd. I think he learned how to be a hockey player this year. Over doubled his production. Hard skill is how I’d describe him. He can fly, he can stickhandle, he can manipulate defenders. He’s a winning hockey player,” Naurato said.

Perron is going to have to continue to prove it as a pro as a 5-foot-9 winger, but he now looks like he’s going to get an entry-level contract. — Scott Wheeler

The Wolverines got a big boost with touted center Michael Hage returning to full action for the Frozen Four semifinal. He missed the regional semifinal because of injury and was the 13th forward for the regional final victory. Hage, a sophomore, will have a decision to make, however, if the Montreal Canadiens indeed try to sign him and have him join the NHL club. Hage, the 21st pick in 2024, had 13 goals and 51 points in 38 games this season for the Wolverines. Hage said he’s taken a big step in his play without the puck, which he knows is needed at the pro level. He said earlier this week he wasn’t letting any NHL thoughts get into his mind while the Wolverines were playing for a title. But Hage has kept a close eye on Montreal during the year. “I watch them as much as I can; they’re a fun team to watch,” he said. “I grew up a fan. It’s pretty special to see how good they’re doing this year.” — Joe Smith
